sentences.t: The problem with this site is what is under it.

Project Cumulus was a hyperscale data center proposed by Clayco and CRG on 440 acres near Elm Point Road and Route 370 in St Charles, in St. Charles County, Missouri, on top of the Elm Point well field that supplies the city's drinking water.

The city's seven wells can produce more than six million gallons a day, but four have been shut down, two of them in 2022 after chemicals from nearby properties got into the groundwater, and the Environmental Protection Agency is overseeing the cleanup.
The end user was never named, described only as a Fortune 100 company, in what project officials called a $1 billion deal.
Spokesman Korb Maxwell told residents: "This is the new base of the economy."
The developers promised water infrastructure upgrades, 50 jobs per building and 700 to 1,000 construction jobs.

Scott Stratton-Henderson, a Lindenwood University student, started an online petition on August 8 that gathered more than 5,000 signatures inside a week, over the diesel that would be stored on the site, flooding, generator noise, emissions, light and traffic.
He said: "Everyone is under a non-disclosure agreement. There is just so much risk as opposed to reward around this project."
The council vote on the conditional use permit had to be moved to the Convention Center on August 19 because so many people came.
The developer withdrew, and then the city shut the door for good.

On May 19, 2026 the city council voted 7 to 1 to add a definition of data centers to the zoning code and to list them as neither a permitted nor a conditional use anywhere in St Charles, making permanent a one year moratorium adopted in the autumn of 2025.
Ward 3 councilman Vince Ratchford called it "a straightforward step that closes a gap in the code and provides clarity for residents, staff, and applicants".
Stratton-Henderson went on to found a nonprofit on accountability, transparency and integrity in the city.
The entry stands as proposed on 440 acres, with no capacity and no cost.
It also shows the city ban dated May 20, 2026 and a St Charles County moratorium running from July 13, 2026 to January 13, 2027.
The 974 megawatt Sioux coal plant is 25 kilometres away.

unconfirmed: Our record held two St Charles entries a kilometre apart, both proposed with no developer; nothing found describes a second Highway 370 data center distinct from Project Cumulus, and they have been merged. The developer is named differently in different accounts: Clayco and CRG in the local magazine, "CRG Cumulus" in the public radio report. Search results also describe the planning and zoning commission approving the site plan but denying the hazardous substance handling permit by one vote on July 14, and a 1.5 million square foot building, which we could not read directly and so have not stated. Both KSDK reports in our record returned HTTP 403. No megawatt or water figure was ever published.

sentences.t: The landowner pulled it himself, a month before the hearing.

On June 26, 2026 Steve Craig, a St Joseph businessman, withdrew the annexation application for a data center at 6321 Southeast Pickett Road, in Buchanan County, Missouri, and the rezoning application for 5701 Pickett Road, both filed through his company Capstone Technology Campus.
The planning commission was to have considered the rezoning on July 23.
Craig gave the reason himself: "We thought that while this debate is going on and underway, we would pause the situation and evaluate other options as well."
The operator would have been Atmosphere Data Centers, run by Chuck McBride, and the design showed four data center buildings and a substation on the site.
Local opposition had organised around the environment, noise and the small number of permanent jobs.
The entry is recorded as cancelled, on 400 acres, with no capacity and no cost.
The acreage does not settle: the annexation covered about 130 acres at one address, with a second parcel to be rezoned, and other accounts describe 300 acres.
Buchanan County has no data center moratorium or zoning limit recorded, and nor does anywhere within reach of it.
This is the only data center site recorded in the county, and there is no other entry within 40 kilometres.

The nearest generators are the 232 megawatt Lake Road gas plant ten kilometres away and two wind farms of 196 and 168 megawatts at 24 and 33 kilometres, with the 1,602 megawatt Iatan coal plant 38 kilometres off.
Atmosphere Data Centers appears elsewhere in the record as the lessee for the Dickerson proposal in Montgomery County, Maryland.

unconfirmed: The acreage is unresolved between our record's 400, the roughly 130 acres described for the annexation parcel, and 300 acres in other summaries; none of those accounts could be read in full. Atmosphere Data Centers' role and the four building layout come from search summaries of the Data Center Dynamics report in our record, which is not fetchable, and are attributed to our record's source list. No megawatt or water figure was published. No resident is quoted here: the report we read carries none, and the opposition is described only in summary. Whether Craig has since refiled, or taken the project somewhere else in Buchanan County, is unknown. The developer fact sheet on the city's own website, also in our record, was not opened.

sentences.t: This one is for sale, and the starting bid was $250,000.

1831 Chestnut Street is a six storey building on 4.24 acres in downtown St. Louis, holding about 53,000 square feet of data center space within roughly 340,000 square feet overall, with two interior generators, one outside, and two Liebert cooling units.
For 32 years it housed Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield's main Missouri data center operations.
The building is in receivership, listed for lease at $15.50 a square foot per floor and put to auction on June 22.
Around it, the city has been writing rules for the first time.
On June 10, 2026 the St Louis Planning Commission approved a zoning framework setting out where data centers may go, how big they may be, and what they must do about energy and noise.

Facilities are sorted by electrical capacity: the smallest may go downtown, in industrial areas and some commercial zones; those between five and 30 megawatts are confined to downtown and industrial land; anything above 30 megawatts is pushed into the most intensive industrial districts, with buffers from homes, schools, transit stops and parks and a conditional use permit for each one.
Ward 1 alderwoman Anne Schweitzer and Ward 7 alderwoman Alisha Sonnier tried to ban the largest outright; the commission rejected the amendment.
Schweitzer said: "We're talking about an unregulated industry that has grown in a way that I don't think we would have wanted it to, based on the intensity of use and the drain on our resources."
The rules apply only to new development, so existing buildings like this one are untouched.
The building is recorded as operating, with no capacity figure and no owner named.
Three other recorded data center buildings sit within a kilometre, and the 486 megawatt Venice gas plant is five kilometres away.

unconfirmed: Three searches were run for this building: 1831 Chestnut with the 340,000 square foot sale and the AT&T building; St Louis data center zoning for June 2026; and the city's board of aldermen restrictions. The building's own details, the receivership, the June 22 auction and the Anthem history all come from search summaries of the Data Center Dynamics report in our record, which is not fetchable, so no source url is given for them. Whether the auction happened and who bought it is unknown. No power capacity is published, and it is not clear how much of the data center space is still in use. No resident objection to this building was found, which is unsurprising for an existing downtown building.

sentences.t: The data center at 210 North Tucker Boulevard in St. Louis is a carrier hotel, the kind of building where networks meet rather than where computing happens at scale.
Netrality owns it along with 900 Walnut Street a few streets away, more than 500,000 square feet between them, bought from Digital Realty in 2016.

The company advertises 20,000 kilowatts of utility power at Tucker with 16,000 kilowatts of backup generation, more than 43 network operators on site, and direct interconnection to its Walnut Street building.
It added two data halls of 11,600 square feet and about 1.2 megawatts of critical capacity in a recent expansion.
The building is recorded as operating with no capacity figure, on the strength of a report about the city considering a moratorium rather than anything about the building itself.
In that report, on September 15, 2025, planning commission head Don Roe wrote that the city needed regulations or should consider a pause while it developed a full understanding of the issue.
Mayor Cara Spencer said she recognised the importance of data centers to biotech, geospatial work, agtech and health care in St Louis.
Ness Sandoval, a sociology professor at Saint Louis University, put the other side: "We don't know what the long-term benefits are."
The rules came nine months later.

On June 11, 2026 the planning commission approved a framework sorting data centers by electrical load, with anything above 30 megawatts pushed into the heaviest industrial districts and buffers required from homes, schools, transit stops and parks.
The rules apply to new development, not to buildings already standing.
Two other recorded data center buildings are at the same coordinates and a third a kilometre away.
The 486 megawatt Venice gas plant is four kilometres off.

unconfirmed: Three searches were run: Netrality with 900 Walnut and 210 North Tucker; St Louis data center zoning for June 2026; and the city's board of aldermen restrictions. The building's own figures, the 20 megawatts of utility power, the network operator count and the data hall expansion, come from the company's marketing pages and directory listings found in search rather than from reporting, and are attributed to our record's source list rather than presented as verified. Our record's only source for this entry is a television report about a possible moratorium which names TierPoint and Netrality as existing operators but gives no detail about this building. No resident objection to it was found.

sentences.t: 900 Walnut Street is the smaller of Netrality's two data center buildings in St. Louis.

The company advertises 13,000 kilowatts of utility power there with 5,000 kilowatts of backup generation, more than 45 network operators, four separate points of entry, and a direct link to its larger building at 210 North Tucker.
Netrality bought both from Digital Realty in 2016 and runs them as carrier hotels rather than as computing campuses.
The building is recorded as operating with no capacity figure.
Its only source is a report from September 15, 2025 about the city considering a moratorium, in which TierPoint and Netrality are named as the operators already downtown.
At that point the city had no rules at all, and planning commission head Don Roe was arguing for either regulations or a pause.
Clifford Spinner, a St Charles resident quoted in the same report, said: "A one-year moratorium is at least a good start."
What the city eventually passed was not a pause.

On June 11, 2026 the planning commission approved a framework that sorts data centers by electrical capacity and confines the largest to the most intensive industrial districts, with buffers from homes, schools, transit stops and parks and a conditional use permit for every project.
City planning executive Miriam Keller called it "open, but very cautious".
Existing buildings, including this one, are not covered.
Two other recorded data center buildings sit at the same coordinates, a fourth a kilometre away, and the 486 megawatt Venice gas plant five kilometres off.

unconfirmed: Three searches were run: Netrality with 900 Walnut and 210 North Tucker; St Louis data center zoning for June 2026; and the aldermen's restrictions. The building's power and connectivity figures come from the company's own pages and directory listings surfaced in search, not from reporting, and are attributed to our record's source list. No reporting about this building specifically exists that we could find; it appears in our record only because a television report named its operator. Its actual load, its tenants and its water use are unknown.

sentences.t: The entry for 3660 Market Street in St. Louis is badly wrong, and the real project is much bigger.
The entry is listed as a TierPoint data center at 3660 Market Street costing $25 million, proposed, with a YouTube clip as its only source.
3660 Market Street is the Armory, a 250,000 square foot complex built in 1938 for the 138th Infantry of the Missouri National Guard, and the data center proposed there is not TierPoint's.
The developers are a local investor, Rod Thomas, and Contour, a Las Vegas property firm.
Their plan is about 500,000 square feet of data center in the old Famous-Barr warehouse next door, with the Armory itself becoming offices.
On April 21, 2026 the city's Board of Public Service unanimously approved the conditional use permits.
The conditions are unusually specific.

Cooling must be a closed loop with air-cooled chillers, the developer must fund a hydraulic model study and pay new water rates set by a cost of service study, at least half the power must be renewable within five years, power usage effectiveness must be 1.25 or better, waste heat must be reported annually, there may be no on-site generators in normal operation, noisy equipment must be enclosed and set back from the frontages, backup must come from batteries, and the roofs must be green, cool or solar.
It must be finished by the end of 2028.

The community benefits agreement puts $15 million, or $30 a square foot, towards transport, digital access and environmental justice, and promises 200 full time jobs, 150 of them in the redeveloped Armory.
The city projects $27.4 million in tax revenue in the first year and $33.4 million for the public schools, and $432.3 million over ten years.

Mayor Cara Spencer said she shared many of the concerns about data centers but that the city had negotiated hard on the ones it could control: "As mayor, I cannot responsibly ignore the amount of good this amount of tax revenue will do for city services, SLPS students and some of the most important amenities and services that our community depends on."
She also said the city would allow data centers only on its own terms, and only if the community benefits.
Not everyone agreed.
Michael Browning argued the project had the potential to be detrimental to the entire city, for its lack of vision, its questionable economic benefit and its heavy demand for energy and water.

The approval came while the city was still writing its zoning rules, and the project, described in the magazine account of those rules as a 120 megawatt data center at the former Famous-Barr warehouse, was exempt from them.

unconfirmed: Our record's name, developer and $25 million cost for this entry do not match anything found at that address, and its only source is a YouTube clip we did not watch; the entry appears to conflate TierPoint, which operates elsewhere in the city, with the Armory and Famous-Barr project. The city's own announcement gives the permit conditions, the jobs and the tax projections but names neither the developers nor a cost; Spectrum News gives $3 billion, and later summaries give $3.1 billion. Rod Thomas and Contour are named only in search summaries. Michael Browning is likewise not named in either report we could read, which says only that opponents watched the meeting from a City Hall conference room. The 120 megawatt figure is a passing reference in the magazine piece rather than a published specification, and the KSDK account returned HTTP 403. Whether construction has started is unknown.

sentences.t: TierPoint's data center at 1111 Olive Street in St. Louis holds more than 124,000 square feet of data center space, and the company advertises cabinet densities of up to 30 kilowatts, the highest in the region.

It is carrier neutral, connected by ten gigabit waves to TierPoint's other sites in Lenexa, Kansas City, Bellevue and elsewhere in St Louis, and came to the company with its acquisition of Cosentry in January 2016.
The building is recorded as operating with no capacity figure, on the strength only of a report about the city considering a moratorium.
That report, on September 15, 2025, named TierPoint and Netrality as the operators already downtown, off 11th and Olive, and described a city with no data center rules at all.
Don Roe, who heads the planning commission, wrote that the city needed regulations or should consider a pause while it worked out what it was dealing with.
City resident Lamont Reynolds was open to it: "I think they should try it, see how it goes."
By the following summer the city had chosen rules over a pause.

The framework approved on June 11, 2026 sorts data centers by electrical load, keeps the smallest downtown, confines those between five and 30 megawatts to downtown and industrial land, and pushes anything larger into the most intensive industrial districts.
An attempt by alderwomen Anne Schweitzer and Alisha Sonnier to ban the largest outright was rejected.
None of it reaches buildings already standing, including this one.
Two other recorded data center buildings are at the same coordinates and a third a kilometre away, with the 486 megawatt Venice gas plant four kilometres off.

unconfirmed: Three searches were run: TierPoint with 1111 Olive; St Louis data center zoning for June 2026; and the aldermen's restrictions. The building's square footage, cabinet density, connectivity and the Cosentry acquisition come from the company's own pages and directory listings surfaced in search rather than from reporting, and are attributed to our record's source list. No megawatt figure is published for the building and no water figure exists. Note that our record holds a second TierPoint entry at 3660 Market Street which does not appear to be a TierPoint project at all.

sentences.t: Because the land is unincorporated, nobody has to vote on this one.

Crusoe, a Denver artificial intelligence company, is proposing a data center in northern Callaway County on land outside any municipality, where a private sale needs no county or public approval and the zoning rules are looser.
The project has grown since the entry was written.

By July 2026 Crusoe was describing a 200 acre, $4.5 billion hyperscale campus, with construction starting between autumn 2026 and summer 2028, 70 permanent jobs at an average of $89,700 a year, and more than 2,000 construction jobs.
The entry still gives 14 acres, with confidence marked low.
Hundreds of people came to an open house at Kingdom City on July 14, 2026.
Crusoe said the cooling would be entirely air-based with no water used for the servers, and declined to give reporters a power figure.

Western District Commissioner Christopher Scott said the county was heading for "zero abatement on real estates, and we're looking like we're going to settle on an 80 percent abatement on the personal property", meaning servers and equipment, and that it was also pressing Crusoe on noise levels and job guarantees.
The company expects to pay more than $100 million a year in real estate tax and to put $15 million into emergency services and healthcare.

Cathy Vogelweide, from Auxvasse, made the point that no tax payment answers: "Because the land going under this will never be farmed again. All the businesses in Callaway County that agriculture support will no longer be necessary when we don't have agriculture."
Residents also raised water use, rising energy costs, noise, and whether the state's Senate Bill 4 protects consumers at all.
The 1,190 megawatt Callaway nuclear station is 30 kilometres from the recorded point, with a 54 megawatt oil plant and a 50 megawatt solar farm both 16 kilometres away.
The only other data center site within 40 kilometres is the Columbia proposal, 34 kilometres off, in a city that has had a moratorium since April 6, 2026.

unconfirmed: The size has changed and our record has not kept up: 14 acres in our record, 200 acres in the July 2026 reporting, with an 800,000 square foot building described in the trade report our record cites, which is not fetchable. The exact location is still unknown and our own record says so, giving only "Northern Callaway Co" at low confidence. Crusoe would not give a power figure. The claim of zero water for server cooling is the company's own and was not independently checked. An earlier gathering of more than 150 residents hosted by the Missouri Protest Organization, at which the water figure of 1.4 million gallons a year was discussed, is known to us only through search results and is not stated above. Whether any land has actually been bought is unknown.

sentences.t: The county's own zoning commission recommended approving this one, and the commissioners did.
On Tuesday, September 15, 2026 the Franklin County Commission voted to rezone two sites for data centers, one of them the Gateway Digital Campus near Villa Ridge, by the Shaw Nature Reserve off I-44.
The other, south of Pacific along Highway O, the zoning commission had recommended refusing.
Residents had spent months on it.

Gene Elkins, who has drawn his water from a well for more than twenty years, said there were "just a lot of questions that never get answered", and that the three commissioners who lead the county seemed set on moving ahead regardless.
He said the opponents thought they had several things that might help them legally, enough to slow it down until what needed taking care of was taken care of, or to stop it.
A Facebook group called No AI Data Centers in Franklin County has more than 3,000 members, and the same group is attached to this entry.
The entry is recorded as under construction on 575 acres, with Provident as the developer and no capacity or cost figure.
An eleven hour planning meeting in the county considered this proposal alongside the Beltline one at Pacific, recommending approval for this and denial for that.
The power is next door.
The 2,372 megawatt Labadie coal plant, one of the largest in Missouri, is nine kilometres away, and the next nearest generator of any size is a 139 megawatt solar farm 53 kilometres off.

Franklin County has no data center moratorium or zoning limit of its own recorded, while the City of St Louis adopted zoning limits on June 10, 2026, the City of St Charles a ban on May 20, and St Charles County a moratorium from July 13.
The three Beltline entries sit nine to ten kilometres away.

unconfirmed: No megawatt, water or cost figure has been published for the Gateway Digital Campus, and no end user has been named. The commissioners' vote count was not reported and no commissioner is named. The eleven hour planning meeting and the split recommendation come from search summaries of Data Center Dynamics and Fox 2 reports that both returned errors, and are attributed to our record's source list. The St Louis Post-Dispatch report in our record redirects to a paywall service and could not be read, so the developer Provident's own account, the acreage and the Shaw Nature Reserve concerns are not described in detail here. Our record says the project is under construction, which sits oddly with a rezoning approved in September 2026; we could not reconcile the two.
